title: The Fountain and the Broken Cisterns
summary: God remembers Israel's early love, when she followed him through the wilderness like a bride, and then brings a legal case against a people who have traded him for worthless idols. They have left the fountain of living water for cracked cisterns, run after Egypt and Assyria for help, and chased other gods like an animal in heat, while insisting they are innocent. God warns that the allies they trust will fail them.
story: After the call in chapter 1, this is Jeremiah's first message, and it sets the tone for the book's opening section (chapters 2 to 6). Before announcing the invasion from the north, God lays out the case against his people. The story he tells runs from the exodus and the wilderness years, through the gift of the land, to the present, and its point is that Israel has no excuse: God did them no wrong, yet they left him. The picture of Israel as God's bride, taken from the prophet Hosea a century earlier, will run through chapters 2 and 3 and leads directly into the call to return in chapter 3.
historical:
Many scholars think this chapter preserves some of Jeremiah's earliest preaching, from the reign of Josiah (about 640 to 609 BC). Verse 18 speaks of going to Egypt to drink the Nile and to Assyria to drink the Euphrates, which assumes Assyria is still a power worth courting; Assyria collapsed between the fall of Nineveh in 612 and its final defeat around 609 BC. Judah's kings had long swung between the two great powers: Ahaz had appealed to Assyria (2 Kings 16), and Hezekiah and later kings looked to Egypt. Verse 36 warns that Egypt will disappoint just as Assyria did.

Verse 16 mentions Memphis, the ancient capital of Lower Egypt near modern Cairo, and Tahpanhes, a frontier fortress in the eastern Nile Delta. The shaving of Judah's head is an image of humiliation. Some connect it with Egypt's control of Judah after Pharaoh Necho killed Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC, which would mean the chapter was updated later; others take it more generally. Tahpanhes is also the place where Jeremiah himself would end up after Jerusalem fell (43:7-9).
cultural:
Water shaped life in the hill country of Judah. A spring, called living water because it flowed, was the best source. Where there was no spring, people cut cisterns into the limestone and plastered them to catch winter rain. A cracked cistern leaked, and whatever water remained went stagnant. To abandon a spring for a cistern was foolish; to dig cisterns that could not even hold water was absurd. That is the image of verse 13.

The worship Jeremiah condemns is Canaanite religion, centered on Baal, the storm god believed to send rain and fertility. Shrines on every high hill and under every green tree were places of worship where sacred poles (representing a goddess) and standing stones (associated with the god) were set up, and ritual sex may have been part of some rites. Verse 27 mocks this: they say to a tree, You are my father, and to a stone, You gave me birth, reversing the expected genders as if to show the confusion. Verses 10 and 11 send the hearers west to Cyprus and east to Kedar, the Arabian tribes of the desert, to see whether any nation there has ever abandoned its gods; even pagans are more loyal to their false gods than Israel is to the true one.
literary: The chapter is poetry built on the form of a covenant lawsuit. The key verb in verse 9, I will contend (riv), is a courtroom word: God brings a case, summons witnesses (the heavens in verse 12, as in Deuteronomy 32:1 and Isaiah 1:2), and answers the defendant's claims of innocence (verses 23 and 35). The chapter piles up metaphors: a bride, firstfruits, a fountain, a slave, a choice vine gone wild, a stain that lye cannot wash out, a young camel and a wild donkey in heat, a thief caught in the act. Rhetorical questions carry the argument (What fault did your fathers find in Me, Has a nation ever changed its gods). A pun links idol and worshiper in verse 5: they followed hevel (breath, emptiness) and became hevel.

outline.t: What fault did your fathers find in Me?
Plundered by the powers they trusted
A wild vine and a runaway animal

doctrines.note: Idolatry is pictured as leaving the fountain of living water for broken cisterns. It is not only worshiping statues but trusting anything else, including foreign alliances, for what only God can give. Idols make their worshipers like themselves: empty.

The chapter reads Israel's history as a marriage covenant: God rescued and led a young bride, and she has been unfaithful. God's case against Judah rests on the covenant obligations the people freely accepted.
Sin here includes denial. The people insist they are not defiled and have not sinned, and God says he will judge them precisely because they say so. Refusing to admit guilt is part of the guilt.

words.note: Chesed, devotion or loyal love. In verse 2 it describes Israel's own love in the early days, the loyalty of a young bride to her husband. It is usually God's chesed that is praised; here God remembers a time when his people returned it, which makes their present faithlessness more painful.

Hevel, breath or vapor, used for what is empty and fleeting (it is the key word of Ecclesiastes, vanity). In verse 5 it names idols: the fathers followed worthless idols and became worthless themselves. The word insists that idols are not evil powers so much as nothing at all, and those who serve them become as empty as their gods.

Riv, to contend or bring a legal case. God uses it in verse 9 (I will contend with you) and the people use it back in verse 29 (Why do you bring a case against Me). The prophets often frame their message as a court case in which God is both plaintiff and judge.

Bor, a cistern or pit, a hole cut in rock to hold rainwater. Set against the fountain of living water in verse 13, the cistern pictures human-made substitutes for God that require great labor and cannot hold what they promise. Later, Jeremiah himself will be thrown into a muddy cistern (38:6).

christ: Jesus takes up the language of living water in John 4:10-14, offering the Samaritan woman water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life, and in John 7:37-39, where he invites the thirsty to come to him and speaks of rivers of living water, meaning the Spirit. Jeremiah calls the LORD himself the fountain of living water; when Jesus offers living water, he claims to give what the prophet said only God gives. The bride imagery also runs forward into the New Testament, where the church is the bride of Christ (Ephesians 5:25-27; Revelation 19:7). Jeremiah's bride has been unfaithful; the New Testament pictures a bride cleansed and made faithful by the husband who gave himself for her. These are thematic connections, not predictions in the chapter, but they are made by the New Testament writers themselves.
questions: God asks what fault the fathers found in him. If God asked you that question, what honest answer might you give about the ways you have drifted?
What broken cisterns are people most tempted to dig today, things that take enormous effort but cannot hold what they promise?
Judah insisted it had not sinned. Why is it so hard to admit wrongdoing, and how does denial make things worse?
